look_here_first: Start with the TWIG, not the leaf: regular corky wings on branches are the fastest clue. Then check whether those wings stop abruptly at a leaf node, look for pointed double-serrate leaves, and use SPRING flowers/samaras to separate winged elm from fall-fruiting cedar elm.

project_inclusion.range_basis: Accepted native Texas species. The completed Rosales deep-review lane locked exact target-zone evidence for Hays, Travis, and Bexar counties; this update reconciles the older provisional learner card with that durable reviewed state.
project_inclusion.range_guardrail: Keep county evidence tied to the reviewed Hays/Travis/Bexar records; do not infer additional counties from statewide range maps alone.

best_field_traits: paired corky wings commonly develop on young and older branches
wings usually terminate abruptly at leaf nodes rather than flowing continuously around them
leaves relatively small, pointed, and double-serrate with pinnate elm venation
flowers before or around leaf-out in spring
small spring samaras with hairy/ciliate margins
morphology_keys.elm_training: Winged elm vs cedar elm: twig wings overlap, so use the node plus season. Winged elm usually has regular wings that end at the node and reproduces in spring; cedar elm may carry corky ridges around nodes and reproduces in late summer-fall.

comparisons.key_distinctions: Cedar elm has rougher blunter leaves and fall flowers/fruit; American elm has much larger asymmetric leaves and normally unwinged twigs; sweetgum has palmately lobed leaves.
